The Harrow Bend Water Reclamation District review examined dosing deviations at polyaluminium chloride feeds across three plants from March 2025 to August 2026, commissioned after Eastfield logged four underdose events in one quarter. About 18 percent of pump fault records were rebuilt from paper logs, and interviews suggested some logs were completed late or backdated. The study compared a fixed 2,000-hour diaphragm replacement schedule with a protocol that replaced diaphragms when stroke-count drift or check-valve pressure decay crossed thresholds. Plants alternated arms by calendar quarter, not randomised by pump. Deviations were readings over 5 percent below setpoint for ten minutes.

The protocol reduced deviations at Eastfield and Northmere, from 0.31 to 0.09 events per pump-month across 1,184 pump-months (95 percent interval 0.14 to 0.27), and the direction held in all four analysed quarters. Deviations clustered in the 72 hours before diaphragm failure, and drift was visible in stroke-count logs two to three weeks earlier, though the flow alarm stayed silent. Saltmarsh showed no significant difference in its first two quarters, so the pattern is not uniform across plants.

Limitations include possible understatement of standard-schedule failures by 4 to 11 percent, a mild winter lowering demand, a single pump model family, and only 11 teardowns validating stroke-count drift as a fatigue proxy. Results may not transfer to sodium hypochlorite or fluoride feeds. Before district-wide adoption, the committee should require validation of the check-valve threshold on another model family and a calibrated flow meter at the injection point. Until then, it should remain a plant-level trial.

The Harrow Bend Water Reclamation District review examined dosing deviations at the polyaluminium chloride coagulant feed systems across its three treatment plants, which serve about 210,000 residents, between March 2025 and August 2026. The review followed four underdose events at the Eastfield plant in a single quarter, each of which prompted a jar test and an assessment for a boil-water advisory that was not issued. Diaphragm metering pump fault records were kept in a shared spreadsheet until early 2025, then moved to a ticketing tool. Pre-migration records were partly rebuilt from paper logs and make up about 18 percent of the analysed records. Operator interviews from May 2026 were used only for context. A deviation was defined as a reading more than 5 percent below setpoint for ten consecutive minutes, taken from the plant historian. Alarms cleared after restarts without a stroke-count check were also counted as deviations.

The investigation compared a standard schedule, which replaced diaphragms every 2,000 operating hours, with a trial protocol, which replaced them when stroke-count drift or check-valve pressure decay crossed engineering-set thresholds. Plants alternated between arms by calendar quarter rather than by randomising individual pumps, so seasonal differences between arms cannot be fully excluded. Each pump-month counted as one unit regardless of run hours, which slightly favours the standard schedule at plants where pumps ran at reduced duty.

The principal finding is that the condition-triggered protocol reduced dosing deviations at Eastfield and Northmere, from 0.31 to 0.09 events per pump-month across 1,184 pump-months. The 95 percent interval for the difference is 0.14 to 0.27. The effect pointed in the same direction in all four quarters analysed at those two plants. A second observation is that deviations clustered in the 72 hours before diaphragm failure. Stroke volume fell gradually without tripping the flow alarm, which is set at a 15 percent band. The drift was usually visible in the weekly stroke-count log two to three weeks earlier, which is why the protocol could intervene before failure.

Several limitations qualify these results. The rebuilt paper records are less complete, and if omitted entries were mostly failures, the standard-schedule deviation rate could be understated by an estimated 4 to 11 percent, which the team could not verify. The study period had a mild winter with lower turbidity and coagulant demand, so deviation counts may partly reflect load. A sensitivity analysis adjusting for turbidity suggested the effect persisted, but the adjusted interval was wide. Some jar tests used samples taken after the rapid mix basin, which may differ from injection conditions, and this was treated as noise and not corrected. Operator log entries may have been backdated, though the extent could not be measured.

The mechanism rests on the assumption that stroke-count drift is a valid proxy for diaphragm fatigue. Only 11 pumps were torn down to test this, and agreement with inspection findings was moderate. Saltmarsh showed no significant difference between arms in its first two quarters. The team attributes this to a chemistry change in the second quarter but did not confirm that explanation. Saltmarsh's result therefore weakens the finding as much as the other two plants support it, and the three-plant pattern should not be treated as uniform. The independent water quality advisor asked for the Saltmarsh analysis to be presented separately, and the advisor's comments are in the committee pack.

The scope is limited to polyaluminium chloride feed at three plants using one pump model family. The results should not be assumed to apply to sodium hypochlorite or fluoride feeds, which have different wear and failure patterns.

The review recommends that before any district-wide adoption, the committee require validation of the check-valve pressure threshold on at least one additional pump model family, and a calibrated flow meter at the injection point, because the current reading depends on the pump's own stroke counter. Until both are in place, the protocol should remain a plant-level trial.

Across three plants serving about 210,000 residents, the Harrow Bend district reviewed dosing deviations in polyaluminium chloride coagulant feeds from March 2025 to August 2026, after Eastfield logged four underdose events in one quarter. A condition-triggered maintenance protocol, which replaces diaphragms when stroke-count drift or check-valve pressure decay crosses an engineering threshold, was compared against a fixed 2,000-hour replacement interval. Plants alternated between arms by calendar quarter rather than by randomisation. At Eastfield and Northmere, the protocol was associated with deviations falling from 0.31 to 0.09 events per pump-month across 1,184 pump-months, with a 95 percent interval of 0.14 to 0.27 for the difference, and the direction held in all four analysed quarters. Saltmarsh showed no significant difference in its first two quarters, and the team attributes this to an unconfirmed chemistry change, so the three-plant pattern should not be treated as uniform. Other caveats include rebuilt paper records making up about 18 percent of the data (possibly understating the standard-schedule deviation rate by 4 to 11 percent), a mild winter that may have lowered load, a stroke-count proxy checked on only 11 pumps with moderate agreement, and scope limited to polyaluminium chloride feeds on one pump model family. Before district-wide adoption, the committee should validate the check-valve threshold on at least one additional model family and install a calibrated flow meter at the injection point; until then, the protocol should remain a plant-level trial.

This report describes an early test of a speech-to-text model intended to draft notes from calls at the Tallowmere contact site, run by a four-person Quillfeather evaluation group. The model was trained on general conversational audio and adapted with a few hundred hours of internal calls, though the adaptation settings are not reproduced because the previous group's configuration log is incomplete. The test set comprised 212 calls from three spring weeks, stratified across billing, repairs, cancellations and general enquiries. Each call was compared against a reference transcript from a trained annotator, but the style guide changed twice, so references were not produced under identical conditions. The mean word error rate was 14.8 percent, ranging from 19.2 percent on billing calls to 11.0 percent on cancellations. The reported interval ignores clustering by agent, so queue differences should be treated as hypotheses. Numerals and product codes made up under a tenth of reference tokens but about a third of substitutions, suggesting the model recovers sound but not number structure. Downstream draft notes were judged acceptable in 71 percent of 140 cases, with modest reviewer agreement. The references were not independently rechecked, which may bias results, especially for digit strings. Results cover only the current headset setup at one site. The group recommends a test of at least 1,000 calls across two sites, a second annotation pass, and a numeral error threshold not yet agreed. Until then, the model should serve only as a drafting aid reviewed by a person.

The evaluation report covers an early test of a speech-to-text model meant to draft notes from recorded calls at the Tallowmere contact site. A four-person group from Quillfeather ran the test. The model was trained on general conversational audio and then adapted with a few hundred hours of internal call recordings. The adaptation settings are not reproduced because the configuration log, written by a previous group, is only partly complete. The speech pipeline was built about eighteen months earlier by a group that has since moved on, and its documentation is partial. Logistics such as meeting schedules, room bookings, and contract payments are mentioned but do not affect the reported numbers; they only explain some delays.

The test set comprised 212 calls from three weeks of spring-quarter recordings, stratified across four queue types: billing, repairs, cancellations, and general enquiries. Each call was transcribed by the model and compared with a reference transcript made by a trained annotator. Annotators heard audio at normal speed only, with replay limited to two passes per segment. The style guide was revised twice during the test, so references were not produced under identical conditions throughout. An August storage reorganisation required manual re-linking of audio files, which took most of a week.

The headline measure was word error rate on normalised text, with numerals, dates, and product codes scored separately. The mean WER across all calls was 14.8 percent (standard deviation 6.1 points). Billing calls averaged 19.2 percent and cancellation calls 11.0 percent. The simple bootstrap interval for the overall mean is about 13.9 to 15.7 percent, but it treats calls as independent and ignores clustering by agent, so the queue-level differences should be treated as hypotheses rather than established results. The clearest pattern is that structured content, namely numerals and product codes, accounts for about a third of substitutions while being under a tenth of reference tokens. This held across all queue types. Reviewers found that many numeral errors were phonetically close to the correct value, such as adjacent digit groups swapped, suggesting the model recovers sound but not number structure.

Calls involved nineteen agents, with a few dominating the sample. One agent with a strong regional accent averaged 22 percent WER, but on only 31 calls, so the figure is unstable. Speaker metadata was restricted to the evaluation team, and the report explicitly offers no judgement about individual agents.

A downstream summariser produced structured draft notes, and two reviewers judged a random subset of 140 as acceptable or not for a customer record. They accepted 71 percent, with modest agreement (kappa 0.48), disagreeing most where a single wrong word changed a request's meaning. This figure is only an approximate guide. The analysis also assumes the reference transcripts are close to ground truth, which was not tested with a second annotation pass. This assumption may be weakest for billing calls, where digit strings were hard to hear, and the direction of any resulting bias is unknown.

The results apply only to the current headset setup at Tallowmere, not to other telephony paths with different compression, and the adaptation data covers a single period, so seasonal effects are unmeasured. The group recommends before any deployment decision a test of at least 1,000 calls across two sites, a second annotation pass on a subset, and a numeral error threshold to be agreed with the operations lead, which has not yet been set. Until then, the model should serve only as a drafting aid reviewed by a person before entering any record. The overall conclusion is tentative: the model may help with draft notes on conversational content, while numeral handling is a weak point that should be addressed first. The next test date has not been fixed.

A simple bootstrap gives an interval of roughly 13.9 to 15.7 percent for the overall mean, but this treats calls as independent and ignores clustering by agent, so the queue-level differences should be regarded as hypotheses rather than established results. The clearest pattern is that structured content, meaning numerals and product codes, accounts for about a third of substitutions while making up under a tenth of reference tokens, and this held across all queue types. Reviewers found many numeral errors were phonetically close to the correct value, such as adjacent digit groups swapped, which suggests the model recovers the sound but not the number structure.

Nineteen agents appear in the calls, with a few dominating the sample. One agent with a strong regional accent averaged 22 percent WER, but across only 31 calls, so that figure is unstable. Speaker metadata was restricted to the evaluation team, and the report explicitly makes no judgement about individual agents.

A downstream summariser produced structured draft notes, and two reviewers judged a random subset of 140 as acceptable or not for a customer record. They accepted 71 percent, with modest inter-rater agreement (kappa 0.48), and disagreed most where a single wrong word changed the meaning of a request. This assumption may be weakest for billing calls, where digit strings were hard to hear, and the direction of any resulting bias is unknown.

The results apply only to the current headset setup at Tallowmere and not to other telephony paths with different compression. Before any deployment decision, the group recommends a test of at least 1,000 calls across two sites, a second annotation pass on a subset, and a numeral error threshold to be agreed with the operations lead, which has not yet been set. Until then the model should serve only as a drafting aid, reviewed by a person before anything enters a record. Until then, the model should serve only as a drafting aid, read by a person before any record is updated.

The Lowmoor Soil Systems Group tested whether low-cost capacitance probes could replace manual gravimetric sampling for scheduling drip irrigation on sandy and clay loams. Across two seasons they installed 214 probes at 31 fields, calibrating each on site against oven-dried samples from four depths. Season one matched gravimetric measurements with a root mean square error of 2.1 percentage points by volume over 9,870 paired observations. An independent second season at 17 fields gave 2.3 points over 6,412 observations. The authors consider this accuracy clearly established.

Probe-scheduled fields applied 14 percent less water than weekly-scheduled controls, a saving replicated in both seasons. Yield differences were not significant, but the 95 percent confidence interval of minus 6 to plus 3 percent cannot rule out a yield penalty of up to six percent. Fewer than half of the fields grew the same crop in both years.

Practical limits include recalibration whenever soil texture changes within a field, and drift in probes installed above a gravel layer below 40 centimetres, which were excluded from water comparisons. Eleven probes failed in season one, mainly from connector corrosion near a wash bay. Salinity was assumed to stay below 2 dS/m but was measured only at installation. A Kell valley pilot reported errors near 5 points, but its raw data are unavailable, so it is treated as a warning rather than a refutation.

All fields were temperate with rainfall above 600 millimetres, mostly rain-fed, so results should not be assumed for arid districts. Only three fields were hilly. Growers should confirm uniform texture or map zones, recalibrate each season, and test salinity separately. The accuracy and water-saving findings are supported, but wider adoption questions remain open.

In season one, probe readings matched gravimetric measurements with a root mean square error of 2.1 percentage points by volume over 9,870 paired observations. An independent second season at 17 fields gave 2.3 points over 6,412 observations. The authors regard this accuracy as clearly established. Probe-scheduled fields applied 14 percent less water than weekly-scheduled controls, a saving replicated in both seasons. Yield differences were not significant, but the 95 percent confidence interval of minus 6 to plus 3 percent cannot rule out a yield penalty of up to six percent. Fewer than half of the fields grew the same crop in both years. Practical limits include the need to recalibrate when soil texture changes within a field and drift in probes installed above a gravel layer below 40 centimetres, which were excluded from water comparisons. Eleven probes failed in season one, mainly from connector corrosion near a wash bay. Salinity was assumed to be below 2 dS/m but was measured only at installation. A Kell valley pilot reported errors near 5 points, but its raw data are unavailable, so it is treated as a warning rather than a refutation. All fields were temperate, with rainfall above 600 millimetres and mostly rain-fed, and only three were hilly, so the results should not be assumed for arid districts. Growers should confirm uniform texture or map zones, recalibrate each season, and test salinity separately. The accuracy and water-saving findings are supported, but questions about wider adoption remain open.

The Lowmoor Soil Systems Group, a small agronomy team at the Tarn Hollow research station in Orrin County, ran a field trial for a regional growers cooperative to test whether low-cost capacitance probes could replace manual gravimetric sampling for scheduling drip irrigation on sandy loam and clay loam fields. Two field technicians, Dara Osei and Pell Varga, handled logistics and rotated between sites every nine days, and principal agronomist Imre Halloran supervised the work and reviewed all calibration data. Across two seasons, 214 probes were installed at 31 fields. Each probe was calibrated on site by a local regression against oven-dried samples from 10, 20, 40 and 60 centimetres depth, with calibration sets collected in the first three weeks of each season and then held fixed. Readings were logged every fifteen minutes to a cooperative server, and the logging scripts were maintained by data engineer Mireille Anand.

The accuracy result was the first principal finding. In season one, calibrated probe estimates matched gravimetric measurements with a root mean square error of 2.1 percentage points by volume across 9,870 paired observations. The second season, run at 17 fields with a fresh probe lot, produced an RMSE of 2.3 percentage points across 6,412 paired observations. Agreement held across both soil textures and all four depths in each season. The authors regard this accuracy result as clearly established because it was reproduced in an independent set of fields and sensors.

The second principal finding concerns water use. Fields scheduling irrigation from probe readings applied on average 14 percent less water than matched control fields on a weekly calendar schedule. Yield differences were not significant in either season. The water saving appeared in both seasons at similar size, so the authors describe it as replicated rather than a single-year effect.

Operational problems occurred. In season one, 11 of 214 probes failed, mostly from corroded cable connectors at a depot stored near a wash bay. Failed units were removed and replaced, and pre-failure data that passed quality checks were kept. The depot was moved in season two, and no failures were recorded there afterward. Technicians also found the mounting tubes hard to seat in stony ground, adding roughly a day per field to installation.

The main practical limit is calibration dependence. Local regressions had to be redone whenever soil texture changed within a field. Probes installed above a gravel layer below 40 centimetres drifted over the season; the team did not correct for this and excluded those probes from the water-use comparison. A grower should map texture before installation rather than assume one calibration covers a whole field.

Growers received a short training session on the dashboard, built by an outside contractor, which showed daily moisture estimates and a simple irrigation trigger. Participants found it easiest to use on phones in the field, though several asked for clearer low-battery warnings. Participants also kept paper irrigation logbooks as a cross-check, which were transcribed into the study database over the winter.

The yield comparison is less certain than the accuracy result. The 95 percent confidence interval for the yield difference ran from minus 6 percent to plus 3 percent, so a modest yield penalty of up to six percent in some crops cannot be ruled out. Fewer than half of fields grew the same crop in both seasons, which widens uncertainty for crop-specific claims.

The analysis also rests on an untested assumption that soil salinity stayed below 2 dS/m across trial fields, since the calibration model was not designed for saline conditions. Salinity was measured once per field at installation and not tracked afterward, so a rise during a season could shift probe readings undetected.

Some prior evidence disagrees. A small pilot the previous year in the neighbouring Kell valley reported errors around 5 percentage points, which it attributed to a different probe lot. The team could not reproduce this because the pilot's raw data were unavailable and its sensors had been discarded, so the pilot should be treated as a warning rather than a refutation until the gap is resolved.

All trial fields were in a temperate climate with annual rainfall above 600 millimetres, and most were rain-fed with supplemental irrigation. Results should not be assumed for arid irrigation districts, where salinity, crusting and deeper root zones may differ. The regional climate gradient was modest, so performance across larger distances was untested. Only three of 31 fields were in hilly terrain, which was too few to draw conclusions about slopes.

Before adopting probe-based scheduling, a grower should confirm uniform soil texture or map it in zones, recalibrate at the start of each season, and check salinity with a separate test. The team recommends completing these steps before expecting any water-use saving. The findings support the accuracy of calibrated probes in temperate loams and the replicated water-saving result, but wider adoption questions remain open.

The Ashgrove Regional Health Trust replaced its outpatient booking module with the cloud-hosted Tessel service between March and July 2026, moving four Wendmoor clinic sites in three waves. The main early work was parsing free-text legacy session records into structured data, with about four percent requiring manual resolution. Dry runs and a daily reconciliation report caught errors, and discrepancies at Eastfield fell from 61 to 4 over nine days. Two early signals came from Eastfield, but both rest on a small, short comparison. The no-show rate rose from 7.1 to 8.4 percent, a 1.3-point change with roughly ±1.9 points of uncertainty. Duplicate bookings fell from 1.9 to 1.2 per hundred, though the legacy counting logic was never reviewed and may not match. Marlow Road showed no no-show change, and Kestrel Court briefly saw higher duplicates. A June survey of Marlow Road online bookers reported 81 percent satisfaction, up from 74 percent for the legacy system, which conflicts with the Eastfield no-show signal. The post-mortem does not recommend changing reminder schedules or retiring the legacy duplicate job yet. It sets three conditions: a quarter-long comparison against a matched control site, a side-by-side duplicate audit of at least 1,000 bookings, and confirmation of consistent no-show coding. Operational lessons include budgeting for manual data cleanup, printed reception guides after cutover, and assigning monitoring ownership early, since the discrepancy report went unreviewed for about three weeks in April. The platform team will extend the Eastfield comparison through the quarter and report to clinical governance in January 2027.

The Ashgrove Regional Health Trust replaced its eleven-year-old outpatient booking module, which ran across four Wendmoor clinic sites, with Tessel, a cloud-hosted scheduling service, between March and July 2026. The legacy system stored bookings in a local database synchronised overnight with the trust's records system. The post-mortem covers how the migration was run, what went wrong at cutover, and early observations about patient attendance. A platform team of six engineers did the technical work, a clinical operations lead owned the decision to cut over each site, and two site managers handled communication with reception staff. The platform team owned data mapping and reconciliation tooling. The largest early problem was converting free-text legacy session strings into structured resources with start times, durations, clinician references and permitted appointment types. About four percent of these strings did not parse cleanly and required manual resolution.

Cutover occurred in three waves: Eastfield first, Marlow Road and Kestrel Court together second, and the orthopaedic referral clinic last because of its complex appointment types. Each wave was preceded by a dry run that loaded the nightly legacy export into a staging copy of Tessel and compared it with the live booking list. A reconciliation script produced a daily discrepancy report counting bookings present in only one system and differences in start time or clinician. Wave one supplied most of the usable data. Over the first nine days after the Eastfield cutover, across 2,300 bookings, daily discrepancies fell from 61 on day one to 4 on day nine, after parsing rules were corrected.

Two findings from Eastfield are reported as early signals only, since they rest on a small, short comparison. First, the no-show rate there reportedly rose from 7.1 to 8.4 percent over the two weeks after cutover, compared with the same weeks a year earlier. The 1.3-point difference has an uncertainty of roughly plus or minus 1.9 points at 95 percent confidence, and it could be explained by the new system, a shift in appointment-type mix, a school holiday, or a change in how no-shows were coded. Second, the rate of duplicate bookings (two active appointments for the same patient and appointment type on one day) fell from 1.9 to 1.2 per hundred bookings. The team tentatively links this to the self-service rebooking flow, which displays existing appointments. This finding is weaker because the legacy duplicate count came from a nightly job whose logic was never reviewed, and the two systems' counting methods have not been confirmed as equivalent.

The pattern did not hold elsewhere. Marlow Road's no-show rate was flat in its first week, and Kestrel Court's duplicate rate briefly rose above pre-cutover levels before settling. The team therefore does not consider Eastfield representative of the trust. A June patient-experience survey added a conflicting signal: of 412 Marlow Road responses, 81 percent rated booking as good or very good, compared with 74 percent for the legacy system in 2025. The survey was voluntary, reached only online bookers, and does not capture telephone bookers, and its direction is in tension with the Eastfield no-show result.

Several untested assumptions affect the analysis. The previous-year baseline may be unreliable because an undocumented rota change occurred at two sites that year. The team also assumed reminders reached a similar share of patients in both periods, but legacy delivery logs were kept for only ninety days and cannot be checked for the baseline.

The post-mortem explicitly does not recommend changing reminder schedules or retiring the legacy duplicate job based on these results. Three conditions should be met first: repeat the no-show comparison over at least a full quarter against a matched control site that stayed on the legacy system; document both systems' duplicate logic and run them side by side on at least 1,000 bookings; and have the clinical operations lead confirm that no-show coding was applied consistently across both periods.

The less contested operational lessons are that field mapping took longer than the vendor estimated and should be budgeted for manual resolution, that dry runs were more valuable than expected because they exposed parsing errors that would otherwise appear as missed appointments, and that reception staff need a printed quick-reference card for roughly the first fortnight after each cutover. The project also exposed an ownership gap: responsibility for the reconciliation report changed hands twice between the platform team and site managers, and for about three weeks in April no one reviewed the discrepancy output. The report now has a named analyst with weekly sign-off. The authors recommend recording ownership of monitoring tools when the systems they monitor are planned. Next steps are that the platform team will extend the Eastfield comparison through the end of the calendar quarter, begin the side-by-side duplicate audit, and report to the trust's clinical governance group in January 2027. Tessel remains live at all four sites, and the legacy module is read-only for historical retrieval. Whether the reminder and duplicate effects are real remains unknown until that extended comparison is complete.

The safety assessment asks whether Harbor Line's 42 autonomous forklifts can share aisles with pedestrian pickers during night operations at the fictional Westgate distribution center. Each unit uses lidar, stereo cameras, and a floor-contact sensor that triggers an emergency stop. The firmware has been updated three times since introduction. Two independent evidence sources were used. A controlled trial of 1,140 scripted mannequin approaches found the emergency stop engaged before contact in about 98 percent of events, with a median stopping distance of 0.9 metres, though only for clean, unobstructed approaches. A retrospective review of 3,870 day-shift operating hours found 37 late or failed stops among 212 near-miss records, likely between 30 and 45, reflecting moderate coder agreement. Fourteen of those involved loaded pushcarts or film-wrapped pallets, which the trial did not test. The field logs lack an approach-event count, so the two rates cannot be compared directly. The trial used one lane with no night conditions and an unloaded grey mannequin. The team concludes the system likely performs well in clear conditions but may underperform with loads or partial occlusion, and it does not recommend sharing night aisles yet. Three conditions must be met first: re-coding field logs against a shared denominator, a second trial with loaded carts and pallets at night lighting, and workshop confirmation that the spring firmware change was tested on those configurations.

The safety assessment evaluates whether Harbor Line's fleet of forty-two autonomous forklifts, built by Orrin Vehicle Works, can share aisles with pedestrian pickers during night operations at the Westgate distribution center near Calder Mills. Each unit has a lidar head, two stereo cameras, and a floor-contact sensor that triggers an emergency stop when a wheel leaves its lane. Site operations lead Dana Pellworth commissioned the review, which was carried out by two site engineers, a contract safety analyst, and a logistics coordinator. The fleet has been in service for two years and has had three firmware updates, covering the lane-marking parser, the speed governor after a spring battery-swap delay, and the stop logic for repeated detections. Maintenance is handled by Tessel Row Service, whose technicians rotate every four weeks. Night shift records are maintained by hand in a spreadsheet, partly transcribed from paper sheets, a factor the team considered when interpreting the data.

Two independent evidence sources were used. A controlled trial of 1,140 scripted approaches on a closed lane, using a dressed mannequin at walking to jogging speeds, found that the emergency stop engaged before contact in 1,118 cases, about 98 percent (95 percent interval roughly 97 to 99 percent), with a median stopping distance of 0.9 metres. This supports reliable stopping when the pedestrian is alone in a clear lane with an unobstructed sensor view. The trial used the nominal speed governor setting, a fixed 220 lux, a matte grey unloaded mannequin, and no night-shift lighting.

The retrospective review coded 3,870 operating hours of the fleet's near-miss logs, but only for the day shift of the previous year, because night logs were incomplete. Two reviewers working separately coded 212 near-miss records, and 37 were classified as late or absent stops with the pedestrian within 1.5 metres. Fourteen of those 37 involved loaded pushcarts or film-wrapped pallets, configurations the trial did not reproduce. Agreement between reviewers was moderate (Cohen's kappa 0.64), with disagreements concentrated in partial occlusion cases behind racks. Because of this uncertainty, the team treats the 37 late stops as a range of roughly 30 to 45.

The two sources cannot be directly compared. The field logs do not record how many pedestrians approached without incident, so no per-encounter failure rate can be calculated, and the trial's 98 percent figure is not comparable to field outcomes. The trial is clean and controlled but narrow, while the field data are messy but reflect real operations. The team's current reading is that the system likely performs well in clear conditions but may underperform with loads or partial occlusion, with the gap concentrated in a small set of configurations whose ranking is not yet reliable. The trial result is therefore treated as a performance ceiling rather than an expected night-floor outcome.

The report does not recommend sharing night-shift aisles with pedestrian pickers at this time. Three conditions must be met first: the field logs must be re-coded against a shared denominator of approach events from both day and night shifts; a second trial must test loaded pushcarts and wrapped pallets at night-floor lighting; and Tessel Row Service must confirm that the spring stop-logic firmware change was tested against those configurations. The review goes to the operations committee, which meets on the first Tuesday of each month, with a follow-up planned for February. Dana Pellworth has asked for a plain-language summary to be shared with the pickers' union representative, and the logistics coordinator will prepare the re-coded spreadsheet once the night logs are complete.

A review of 212 day-shift near-miss records found 37 late or failed stops, estimated at roughly 30 to 45 given moderate coder agreement, and fourteen of those involved loaded pushcarts or wrapped pallets that the trial did not reproduce. The field logs lack an approach-event denominator, so the two rates cannot be compared directly. The report does not recommend sharing night aisles now and treats the trial as a performance ceiling. Three conditions must be met first: re-coding field logs against a shared denominator, a second trial with loaded carts, pallets, and night lighting, and confirmation that the spring stop-logic firmware was tested on those configurations.

This safety assessment reviews whether the Harbor Line fleet of forty-two autonomous forklifts, built by Orrin Vehicle Works, can share aisles with pedestrian pickers during night operations at the Westgate distribution center. The review was commissioned by site operations lead Dana Pellworth after night-shift supervisors requested a clear answer before pedestrian zones were extended. Two evidence sources were used. A controlled trial of 1,140 scripted approaches on a closed test lane found the emergency stop engaged before contact in about 98 percent of events (95 percent interval roughly 97 to 99 percent, median stopping distance 0.9 metres), but only for clean approaches with an unobstructed sensor view. A retrospective review of 3,870 day-shift operating hours coded 212 near-miss records, of which 37 were late or missed stops with the pedestrian within 1.5 metres; 14 of those involved loaded pushcarts or film-wrapped pallets, which the trial did not reproduce. Inter-reviewer agreement was moderate (Cohen's kappa 0.64), so the 37 figure should be read as roughly 30 to 45. The two sources cannot be directly compared because the field logs have no count of approach events to serve as a denominator, and the trial used a matte-grey unloaded mannequin at a fixed 220 lux with no night lighting tested. The team's current reading is that the system likely performs well in clear conditions but may underperform with loads or partial occlusion, and the report does not recommend sharing night aisles at this time. Three conditions must be met first: re-coding the field logs against a shared denominator covering both shifts, a second trial including loaded pushcarts and wrapped pallets at night-floor lighting, and confirmation from the maintenance workshop that the spring stop-logic firmware change was tested against those configurations. The review goes to the operations committee, with a follow-up planned for February.

A university lab, the Cell Durability Group, tested for a regional transit authority whether cheaper cell chemistries could safely replace current packs in a shared e-bike fleet. It cycled 214 complete packs from four production lots by two makers, using a commuter profile with 80 percent depth of discharge and 2 C fast charging, at 25 or 35 degrees Celsius, up to 1,200 cycles. Capacity was checked every 50 cycles at 0.5 C.

Lithium iron phosphate packs retained a median 81 percent of rated capacity at 1,000 cycles at 25 degrees, against 68 percent for nickel manganese cobalt packs, a gap present in all four lots. An eight-month replication with 96 fresh packs reproduced the ordering (80 and 66 percent), but used the same group and profile. The 35 degree chamber ran only 400 cycles after a cooling failure, so hot-condition claims are indicative only. The confidence interval on the difference is roughly 9 to 15 percentage points, though it treats packs within a lot as independent and may understate spread.

Results apply only to packs without active thermal management and to commuter use; delivery loads and sub-freezing climates were untested. A transit log of 60 bikes showed no clear range-complaint difference but lacks cycle counts, so it cannot be reconciled with the bench data. The group recommends a thermal review and a pilot in the intended climate before any changeover, with purchase contracts specifying capacity tests at field-like discharge rates.

The Cell Durability Group at Halden Ridge Institute of Electrified Transport, a university-affiliated lab in Pell Harrow, ran a benchmark commissioned by a regional transit authority to determine whether lower-cost cell chemistries could safely replace the current packs in its shared e-bike fleet. The project extended a three-year bench study of single cells to complete packs in purpose-built housings. The team had five members: a principal investigator who handled the contract, a senior technician who ran the environmental chambers, two graduate students who managed cycling and data cleaning, and a part-time statistician who reviewed the analysis plan but did not visit the site. Much of the first year went to logistics, including two chamber recalibrations and a seven-week customs hold on one shipment of packs.

Testing covered 214 packs from four production lots supplied by Corvane Cell Works and Ostrava Field Power. Each pack ran a commuter profile at 80 percent depth of discharge with 2 C fast charging for the first 60 percent of each charge, for up to 1,200 cycles or until capacity fell below 70 percent of rated value. Chambers held 25 degrees Celsius and 35 degrees Celsius. Capacity was checked every 50 cycles with a 0.5 C reference discharge, which is slower than typical rider draw. Two packs were removed for a connector fault unrelated to cell behaviour, leaving 212 in the first wave. The in-house logging software changed version midway through, and a comparison of twelve packs under both versions showed identical outputs within measurement noise. Cycling was scheduled in overnight blocks, packs were rotated between shelf positions every two weeks, and a few swaps were missed during a cooling failure. The analysis used a mixed model with lot as a random effect, fitted to capacity retention at each checkpoint, with medians taken from the fitted curves. Packs reaching 70 percent were treated as ending at that cycle, and packs still running at 1,200 cycles were censored. The team estimated lithium iron phosphate packs were about 18 percent cheaper per kilowatt hour at purchase, though regional prices were volatile.

The principal finding is that at 1,000 cycles under the 25 degree condition, lithium iron phosphate packs retained a median of 81 percent of rated capacity, compared with 68 percent for nickel manganese cobalt packs. The gap held across all four lots. A replication wave of 96 fresh packs from a third lot, run eight months later, reproduced the ordering with medians of 80 and 66 percent. Because the same group ran both waves with the same profile, the replication shows repeatability within this design rather than independence from it. The 95 percent confidence interval on the median difference is roughly 9 to 15 percentage points. The interval treats packs within a lot as independent, which the authors acknowledge may understate the spread, and it cannot exclude a smaller effect for real riders.

The 35 degree chamber ran only 400 cycles because of a cooling failure in the second half of the year, so conclusions about hot conditions rest on a much shorter record. The group describes that data as indicative only and has not published a comparison at matched cycle counts.

The results apply only to packs without active thermal management and to commuter use. The study did not test heavier delivery loads or cold climates below freezing, where lithium iron phosphate behaviour may differ. The team also assumed the 0.5 C reference discharge reflects usable field capacity, which has not been verified on these packs. A short bench check on eight packs was planned but was unfinished at report time. A separate transit authority field log covering 60 bikes over six months showed no clear difference between chemistries in range complaints, but riders described range by feel and the log lacks cycle counts, so it cannot be reconciled directly with the bench data. The group recommends a thermal management review and a pilot in the intended climate before any changeover, and purchase contracts that specify capacity testing at discharge rates closer to field use. The graduate students who maintained the tracking spreadsheet left the project in spring, and their handover notes are archived with the raw logs.

The gap held across four production lots and was reproduced in a 96-pack wave from a third lot (80% versus 66%), but both waves used the same group and profile, so this shows repeatability within the design rather than independent confirmation. The 95% interval on the median difference is roughly 9 to 15 points, computed treating packs within a lot as independent, which the authors say may understate spread. Hot-condition results are indicative only: the 35°C chamber ran just 400 cycles after a cooling failure. Capacity was measured at a 0.5 C discharge rate, which riders seldom draw, and its link to real-world range was not checked. A separate transit field log of 60 bikes showed no clear range-complaint difference but lacks cycle counts, so it cannot be reconciled with the lab data. Findings apply only to packs without active thermal management, to commuter use, and to temperatures above freezing. Before any changeover, the authority should require a thermal management review and a pilot in its intended climate, and any purchase contract should specify capacity testing at a discharge rate closer to field use.

This review assesses whether a lithium iron phosphate pack can replace lead acid strings in trackside signal cabinets on the Eastmere branch line without changing cabinet footprint. The Signalling Power Group requested it after spring outages at Millbrook crossing, later traced to a faulty contactor. Their standby requirement fell from four hours to ninety minutes after a junction upgrade, but approval records are incomplete, so ninety minutes is treated as a working figure rather than a verified one.

The evaluation rests on a bench test of two prototype cabinets over eleven weeks at Harrowgate Junction depot, with forty discharge events drawn from logged operating data. The lithium pack sustained the required ninety minutes in all forty events, while the lead acid reference fell short in nine. Prototype capacity varied about eleven percent, and cold January conditions were not reproduced. The discharge events were not randomised.

The design assumes feeder charger voltage stays within the window taken from a comparable pack datasheet, and it was measured only once at the four stations.

The panel judges the option promising but unestablished and recommends a second test campaign. Adoption should await a quarter of continuous feeder voltage logs at every station, winter thermal measurements, and fault data re-coded by cabinet. Until then, lead acid strings should remain in service.

The design review assesses whether a lithium iron phosphate battery pack can replace the lead acid strings in the trackside signal cabinets on the fictional Eastmere branch line, which serves four rural stations, without changing cabinet footprint. The Signalling Power Group requested the review after short outages at the Millbrook crossing, which were later traced to a faulty contactor rather than the supply design. The lead engineer, Renata Oyelaran, asked that the review focus on the replacement question. Procurement history and the vendor shortlist are held in the group's document store and are not included.

The cabinets date from the late nineteen nineties and have been refurbished twice. The original specification required four hours of standby from a lead acid string, but a later revision reduced this to ninety minutes after a signal upgrade at the junction. Records do not confirm who approved that change, so the review treats ninety minutes as a working requirement, not a verified one.

The evaluation rests on a bench test of two prototype cabinets run over eleven weeks at the Harrowgate Junction depot. The prototypes were loaded with a simulated demand profile based on logged operating data and went through forty discharge events of varying depth. With only two cabinets, the results describe a narrow range of conditions and are not a population estimate. Three groups shared responsibility: the Depot Test Bay team ran the rig and daily checks, the Asset Analysis team owned fault data, and the Signalling Power Group owned the design and recommendation. The minutes note that handover of the logger calibration sheet took longer than planned.

The in-house logging software, written by the Tooling Office, exports comma separated data. The logger clock drifted about four seconds per day for part of the trial, which was corrected in post-processing. Some rows were dropped in an October export due to a buffer setting and were recovered from a backup. The recovery was checked by comparing totals only, not row by row.

The main finding is that the lithium pack sustained the required ninety minutes in all forty events, while the lead acid reference string fell short in nine. The review suggests the lithium arrangement may reduce unplanned site visits, but this is an inference from a short test and is unconfirmed in the field.

Charge retention estimates carry wide uncertainty. Measured capacity varied by about eleven percent between the two prototypes, and the confidence interval on end of discharge voltage spans roughly 0.3 volts. Neither figure rules out a meaningful difference from the reference string at the lower January temperatures, which the bench could not reproduce because the test bay heater was out of service for three weeks. The forty events were not randomised: eighteen ran in summer and twenty-two in autumn. The seasonal comparison was not planned in advance and is included only to show the result does not depend entirely on one season.

A separate desk study by Asset Analysis, using fault records from four other branch lines, found a lower failure rate for lead acid cabinets than the bench results predict. Those records are kept by visit rather than by cabinet, so the sources are not directly comparable, and the study's authors had not seen the bench data when drafting.

The prototypes were moved to the depot on a hired flatbed in July and reinstalled within two days. Two cooling fans were replaced under warranty during the trial, and the dates are in the maintenance log.

The design assumes the existing feeder's charger output stays within the window the lithium management system expects. That window comes from a datasheet for a comparable pack and has not been checked against actual feeder voltage at the four stations, which was measured once, in August, by the field survey team.

Three conditions should be met before adoption: continuous feeder voltage logging for at least one full quarter at every station, winter thermal measurement in the test bay, and fault data re-coded by cabinet for direct comparison with the bench results. If any is unmet, the recommendation should be treated as provisional and the lead acid strings kept in service. Overall, the review judges the lithium option promising but not yet established, recommends a second test campaign before any procurement decision, and notes the final figures may change once field logs are complete.

This design review assesses whether a lithium iron phosphate battery pack could replace the lead acid strings in the trackside signal cabinets on the fictional Eastmere branch line without changing cabinet footprint, a question raised by the Signalling Power Group after spring outages at Millbrook crossing that were later traced to a faulty contactor. A desk study of fault records from four other branch lines suggested a lower lead acid failure rate than the bench predicted, but it counts faults by visit rather than by cabinet, so the sources are not directly comparable. The design assumes the feeder charger voltage falls within the window the lithium management system expects; that window comes from a comparable pack's datasheet and was measured at the four stations only once. The panel makes adoption conditional on continuous feeder voltage logging for a full quarter at every station, a winter thermal test in the bench, and fault data re-coded by cabinet. Until those are met, the panel calls the lithium option promising but unestablished, recommends a second test campaign, and says existing lead acid strings should stay in service.

Until then, the lead acid strings should remain in service, and a second test campaign is recommended before any procurement decision.

This two-winter field study by the Tallow Ridge Energy Group, with installer Brightwater Fitting Co. and utility Halden Power Cooperative, examined whether home batteries reduce evening grid imports for households with rooftop solar. Between March and August 2024, 4,312 households received a 9.6 kWh battery and 4,198 solar-only households served as comparisons. In the first winter, battery households cut grid imports from 17:00 to 22:00 by 41 percent (95% CI 39 to 43), using a difference-in-differences model. A second winter in a separate district with 1,106 households showed a 38 percent reduction. The study was not randomised, and matching on fourteen covariates reduced but did not eliminate baseline imbalance, so unmeasured motivations may matter. The results depend on Halden's tariff, which has a 17:00 to 21:00 peak at 0.31 per kWh; a flat tariff was not tested. A summer sub-study of 212 households suggested about 12 percent (CI roughly 2 to 22), which the team treats only as a hypothesis. Lifetime economics rely on a manufacturer degradation rate of 2.1 percent per year, untested beyond an 18-month record. A 2023 pilot of 88 households found 19 percent, and the team suggests that inverter discharge limits below 2 kW explain much of the gap, though this is unproven. Before acting, the team advises confirming that inverters discharge at least 3 kW, that the tariff has a meaningful evening premium, and that warranty terms match the degradation assumption. Cost-effectiveness was not assessed, since the study measured imports rather than bills. A third winter with a flat-tariff arm is planned, with a funding decision expected in Q1 2027. The raw data are held by the cooperative and are not public.

The Tallow Ridge Energy Group, a small applied research team in Merrow Fell, Ardane, carried out a two-winter field study of home batteries in households that already had rooftop solar. Enrolment ran from March to August 2024. Brightwater Fitting Co. handled hardware installation, and the Halden Power Cooperative supplied 15-minute interval meter data under a research agreement. The study compared 4,312 households that received a 9.6 kWh lithium battery with 4,198 solar-only households. All homes had 3 to 7 kW systems and interval meters. The question was how much a battery reduced grid imports during the evening peak, 17:00 to 22:00, when the cooperative's time-of-use tariff charges the most.

In the first winter, battery households reduced evening grid imports by 41 percent relative to matched comparison households (95 percent CI 39 to 43 percent). The estimate came from a difference-in-differences model with standard errors clustered by postcode. A second winter in a separate district of 1,106 households showed a 38 percent reduction, which the team attributes to ordinary between-district variation. The study is observational, not randomised. Households opted into batteries, and unrecorded motivations may differ between groups. Matching on fourteen covariates reduced the baseline imbalance in evening use (standardised mean difference from 0.31 to 0.06), but it cannot adjust for unmeasured factors. The second district was chosen partly for convenience, and its households had slightly newer inverters, which the report later identifies as relevant. Pre-installation trends in the comparison group tracked the treated group within the noise of the data.

The results depend on the tariff. Halden's evening peak runs 17:00 to 21:00 at 0.31 currency units per kWh, with a flat off-peak rate. The study did not test a flat tariff, a steeper one, or different peak timing, so the 41 percent figure should not be assumed to transfer to markets with a small peak premium.

A one-month summer sub-study of 212 households gave a point estimate of about 12 percent, with a wide interval of roughly 2 to 22 percent. The team does not treat this as established and presents it as a hypothesis for future work. The findings apply to winter only.

The lifetime economics rely on an untested assumption. The cost model uses the manufacturer's degradation curve, which projects about 2.1 percent capacity loss per year. The longest field record is eighteen months, so ten-year performance is extrapolated. Faster degradation would reduce the evening savings implied by the winter results.

A 2023 pilot by another group, with 88 households in a neighbouring region, found only a 19 percent evening import reduction. Those households had inverters capped below 2 kW discharge. The team's sub-analysis suggests discharge rate explains much of the difference, but this is plausible rather than proven, since the older study did not record inverter models.

The report sets three conditions before acting on these results. Target inverters should discharge at no less than 3 kW, because the team's dose-response check found the benefit levelled off below that value. The tariff should carry a meaningful evening peak premium. The purchaser should check battery warranty terms against the degradation assumption. The study measured grid imports, not bills, so it does not assess cost-effectiveness.

A third winter with a flat-tariff arm is planned, pending a provincial grant decision expected in Q1 2027. Data cleaning for this report took about five months, mainly to reconcile meter timestamps across two firmware versions. The raw data are held by the cooperative and are not publicly released.

The Ferndale Coast Analytics group audited the nightly sales forecasting feed that supplies weekly volume estimates to replenishment planners for 118 stores in the fictional Saltmere region. The feed was rebuilt in March, when it moved from the Tidewell batch scheduler to a streaming service called Breakwater. That migration was delayed twice, once by a certificate renewal and once by a dispute over how promotional codes should be represented in the schema. Three analysts carried out most of the audit, often in evenings and on weekends. Because planners order weekly, even a shift of a few percent can change order quantities for slow-moving lines.

The audit asked whether the feed's weekly totals match actual sales and, if they do not, where the difference begins. It compared against two sources: the store ledger, a nightly point-of-sale export that finance reconciles monthly, and the regional rollup, a dashboard aggregate built from the same terminals but sent through a separate transport path with its own buffering. The team treated any disagreement between these sources as something to explain, not as proof of error. The core evidence came from a stratified sample of 52 stores, chosen in proportion to the three size tiers' share of weekly volume. Nine weeks of raw terminal events for those stores were replayed through a staging copy of the feed, and the replayed totals were compared with both sources. The replay was the only step that isolated the feed from other systems, so it carries most of the weight of the report.

Breakwater converts each terminal event's local time offset to a universal timestamp and then applies a closing-time rule, defined in an operations configuration file, that assigns any event stamped after 22:00 local time to the following business day. The rule was written for stores closing at 21:00, and several sampled stores stay open later on weekends. The team found that the rule's interaction with terminal clock offsets had never been tested as a combined case. Validation ran in three passes. A row-count check found no dropped rows, ruling out simple ingestion loss. A comparison for one problem store against the ledger showed discrepancies on the same days as late-evening events. A comparison for a store without clock issues showed no discrepancy. These passes point toward the timestamp rule, but none tests it directly.

The principal finding is that transactions stamped after a store's closing time are assigned to the next business day, moving about 1.8 percent of weekly volume from one week into the next in the sample. The effect concentrates in stores whose terminal clocks were set to a different time zone during the March migration. Replay reproduced the shift in 38 of the 52 stores, which is the strongest single piece of evidence.

The ledger comparison supports this only partly. Feed weekly totals agree with the ledger within 0.3 percent for 41 stores, and the remaining eleven show differences that reverse sign week to week, consistent with a timing shift. The regional rollup shows a different pattern. In the western cluster of 14 stores, it reports a persistent undercount of about 2.6 percent that does not reverse and does not appear in the ledger. The team suspects the rollup's buffering, which can hold events for up to 40 minutes, but has not confirmed this. The audit therefore could not determine whether the western undercount stems from a feed fault, a rollup fault, or a real difference in how late-evening sales are buffered. The estimate of this persistent gap has a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 1.1 percent, too wide for planning use without a second data source.

Several limits apply. The nine-week window is short for a feed serving a full fiscal year, seasonal promotions fell outside it, and the forecasting model that consumes the feed was not examined, so the report makes no claim about forecast accuracy. The ledger is reconciled only monthly, so the final two weeks of comparison used unreconciled figures. The analysis also assumes all terminals in a store share one clock source, which was verified for only six stores against a network time service. Before changing the feed, the team recommends verifying the timestamp rule against two full fiscal months of ledger data and re-examining the western cluster with the rollup transport path disabled. Until both checks are complete, planners should treat weekly figures as accurate only to within about three percent.

Other details did not alter the conclusions. Log access went through a change board meeting on alternate Thursdays, adding about a week. The regional dashboard belongs to a separate group that was busy with a quarterly reporting cycle. Earlier migration-period audit notes found in a shared folder were excluded because they describe an older version of the feed, and their style resembles current change records, so they are easy to confuse with them. The staging copy was refreshed twice, and both refreshes were logged in the team's change record.

In a stratified sample of 52 stores over nine weeks, this shifts about 1.8% of weekly volume into the next week, concentrated in stores whose terminal clocks were set to a different time zone during the migration. Replaying raw events through a staging copy reproduced the shift in 38 of the 52 stores, which the report treats as the strongest evidence. Ledger comparison only partly supports this: feed totals agreed with the ledger within 0.3% for 41 stores, and the other eleven showed sign-reversing differences consistent with timing shifts. Separately, the regional rollup showed a persistent undercount of about 2.6% in a 14-store western cluster that the ledger did not show. The auditors could not determine whether that gap originates in the feed, the rollup's buffering (which can hold events up to 40 minutes, unconfirmed), or real differences in late-evening sales; its 95% interval is ±1.1%.

The report's limits are substantial. The sample covers nine weeks, excludes seasonal promotions, does not evaluate the forecasting model, and relies on monthly-reconciled ledger data for its final two weeks. The single-clock-source assumption was checked for only six stores. Validation was three small passes that point toward the timestamp rule but do not test it directly. Before any change to the feed, the team recommends verifying the timestamp rule against two full fiscal months of ledger data and re-examining the western cluster with the rollup transport path disabled. Until then, planners should treat weekly figures as accurate only to within about three percent.

The Ferndale Coast Analytics audit asked whether the nightly sales forecasting feed's weekly totals match actual sales for 118 Saltmere stores, following a March migration from the Tidewell scheduler to the Breakwater streaming service. The team replayed nine weeks of raw terminal events for a stratified sample of 52 stores and compared results with a monthly-reconciled store ledger and a regional rollup dashboard. The principal finding is that transactions stamped after a store's local closing time are assigned to the following business day, moving about 1.8 percent of weekly volume between weeks, concentrated in stores whose terminal clocks were set to a different time zone during migration. Replay reproduced the shift in 38 of 52 stores. The ledger supports this only partly: 41 stores agree within 0.3 percent, and eleven show sign-reversing differences consistent with timing shifts. A persistent 2.6 percent undercount in the western cluster of 14 stores appears in the rollup but not the ledger, and its cause remains unresolved, with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 1.1 percent. Limits include the nine-week window, the unexamined forecasting model, two unreconciled ledger weeks, and clock sharing verified in only six stores. Before any change, verify the timestamp rule against two full fiscal months of ledger data and re-examine the western cluster with the rollup buffering disabled; until then, planners should treat weekly figures as accurate only to within about three percent.

A nightly sales forecasting feed for 118 Saltmere stores was audited after its March migration from the Tidewell batch scheduler to the Breakwater streaming service, to determine whether its weekly totals match actual sales and, if not, where the difference starts. The principal finding is that the feed assigns transactions stamped after a store's local closing time to the following business day. Its closing-time rule, written for 21:00 closers, was never tested against terminal clock offsets. In the sample, this shifts about 1.8% of weekly volume into the next week, concentrated in stores whose terminal clocks were set to a different time zone during migration. Replaying raw events reproduced the shift in 38 of 52 sampled stores. Validation was indirect, since no pass tested the rule itself, and the ledger and regional rollup comparisons were only partly consistent with this explanation.

Against the store ledger, feed totals agreed within 0.3% for 41 of 52 stores, and the other eleven showed sign-reversing differences consistent with a timing shift. In the 14-store western cluster, the regional rollup showed a persistent undercount of about 2.6% that the ledger did not show. The team suspects the rollup's buffering but has not confirmed it, and the 95% interval on that gap is ±1.1%, so the team could not attribute it to the feed, the rollup, or real sales timing.

The sample covers nine weeks, excludes seasonal promotions, does not examine the forecasting model, and makes no claim about forecast accuracy. Its final two weeks relied on unreconciled ledger data, and the assumption of one clock source per store was checked for only six stores. Before any feed change, the team recommends verifying the timestamp rule against two full fiscal months of ledger data and re-examining the western cluster with the rollup transport disabled. Until then, planners should treat weekly figures as accurate only to within about 3%.

The Marrowdale regional hospital network's clinical engineering office commissioned the Ostrander Field Group, an unfunded-by-vendor team, to test whether the occlusion alarm on its volumetric infusion pumps responds within the network's 20-second acceptance limit. The team used a bench rig with a gravity-fed saline reservoir, a pneumatic clamp about 40 cm downstream, and logging of line pressure and alarm timing. Fourteen pumps from three hardware revisions were tested with operators blinded to revision. Revision C, which has a revised pressure filter and shortened firmware detection window, accounted for 2,160 trials across three campaigns. Revisions A and B served as comparison arms in one campaign only.

Revision C met the 20-second limit in 96.9 percent of trials, compared with 88.4 percent for revision A and 91.2 percent for revision B. The result held across the three campaigns, at 96.7 to 97.4 percent. The advantage was largest at abrupt closure and high flow. Those latency medians used only trials in which an alarm sounded. The 95 percent interval was 96.2 to 97.7 percent, likely understated because trials on the same unit were not independent.

Two ward occlusions with alarm delays over 30 seconds remain unexplained, as the bench could not reproduce them and reports omitted tubing and flow rate. Testing used only room-temperature saline, so results do not cover viscous fluids, lipids, or air. Closure rates were chosen from published notes and staff discussion, not patient measurements. Only one rig was built, so variation between rigs was not estimated.

The team recommends not relying on these results for high-viscosity infusions until a viscous-fluid study is complete. Before clinical rollout, the firmware should be tested on at least two independent rigs, and ward incident reports should be re-reviewed with flow rate and tubing recorded.

The bench study, commissioned by the clinical engineering office of the Marrowdale regional hospital network, tested whether the occlusion alarm on its general-purpose volumetric infusion pumps responded quickly enough when a downstream line became blocked. The Ostrander Field Group carried out the work, with a lead engineer coordinating the protocol, two technicians running the rigs on alternating shifts, and a biostatistician from the network's quality office reviewing the analysis plan before data collection. The protocol was fixed before the first trial and was later checked against a dated file. No device manufacturer funded the study, and the team had no vendor contract during the period.

The rig used a gravity-fed saline reservoir, a carriage holding each pump at a fixed height, standard administration tubing, and a pneumatic clamp about 40 cm downstream of the pump outlet. The clamp closed at three controlled rates (slow, moderate, abrupt) to imitate different blockages. A pressure transducer logged line pressure at 50 samples per second, and a timer recorded the interval from clamp closure to the first alarm. Each trial began with two minutes of running at a set rate to reach steady state. The clamp was cleaned and leak-checked each session, and trials with a visible connector leak were discarded and repeated.

Fourteen pump units from three hardware revisions (A, B and C) were tested. Revision C, which has a revised pressure filter and a shortened firmware detection window, accounted for all 2,160 trials in the main analysis, spread over three campaigns in different months of 720 trials each. Each campaign covered five flow rates, three tubing sets and the three closure rates. Revisions A and B were run only in the first campaign as comparison arms, with 360 trials each. The rig was recalibrated against a reference gauge before every session, and revision labels were covered until data were locked so operators were blind to revision.

The principal finding is that revision C raised its alarm within the network's 20-second acceptance limit in 2,094 of 2,160 trials, or 96.9 percent. In the first campaign, revisions A and B met the same limit in 88.4 and 91.2 percent of comparison trials. The advantage was greatest at the abrupt closure rate and highest flow setting, where median alarm latency fell from about 17 seconds to about 9 seconds. These medians used only trials in which an alarm sounded.

The result replicated across the three campaigns. Revision C met the limit in 697, 701 and 696 of 720 trials, giving rates of 96.8, 97.4 and 96.7 percent. The spread was small, and no single campaign drove the overall result. Treating trials as independent, the 95 percent interval for the within-limit rate was 96.2 to 97.7 percent. Because trials on the same unit were not fully independent, the true interval is probably somewhat wider.

The team also reviewed ward incident reports. Between revision C's release and the study's end, one ward logged two occlusions in which the alarm sounded more than 30 seconds after a nurse noticed flow had stopped. The team could not reproduce delays of that size on the rig, and the reports did not record tubing set or flow rate, so whether bench conditions matched the ward could not be determined. The team treated these reports as unresolved.

All trials used room-temperature normal saline. Blood, lipid emulsions and other viscous fluids were not tested, and the findings do not address behaviour with thickened fluids or air in the line. The closure rates were chosen to approximate blockage dynamics believed to be typical, based on published test notes and discussion with network anesthesia staff, and this choice was recorded in the protocol beforehand. Real patient blockage pressure curves were not measured, so the assumption that the closure rates bracket clinical conditions remains untested. Only one rig was built, so variation between rigs was not estimated; a second rig would have added about three weeks of setup and was judged acceptable only for the final decision.

The team recommends that the network not rely on these results for high-viscosity infusions until a separate viscous-fluid campaign is completed. Before any clinical rollout, revision C firmware should be run on at least two independent rigs, and ward incident reports should be re-reviewed with flow rate and tubing set recorded.

The quality office reviewed the report internally, and it went to the network's pump committee in late summer. The committee requested the raw transducer logs, which were provided as a sealed archive, and a two-page plain-language summary for ward managers, which is not reproduced in the report. The rig was moved to storage after the final campaign and has since been recalibrated, which does not affect the results.

No device manufacturer funded the work, and the team had no vendor contract during the study period. The rig used a gravity-fed saline reservoir, a height-fixed pump carriage, standard tubing, and a pneumatic clamp about 40 cm downstream of the pump outlet that closed at slow, moderate, or abrupt rates. A pressure transducer sampled at 50 Hz and a timer measured the interval from clamp closure to first alarm. Each trial began with two minutes of running for steady state, and trials with visible connector leaks were discarded and repeated. Fourteen pump units from three hardware revisions (A, B, and C) were tested. Revision C, which has a revised pressure filter and a shortened firmware detection window, supplied all 2,160 trials in the main analysis across three campaigns of 720 trials each, covering five flow rates, three tubing sets, and the three closure rates. Revisions A and B were compared only in the first campaign, with 360 trials each. The rig was recalibrated before every session, and revision labels were hidden from operators until data were locked.

The principal finding is that revision C raised its alarm within the network's 20-second acceptance limit in 2,094 of 2,160 trials, or 96.9 percent. In the first campaign, revisions A and B met the limit in 88.4 and 91.2 percent of comparison trials. The advantage was largest at the abrupt closure rate and highest flow setting, where median alarm latency dropped from about 17 seconds to about 9 seconds; these medians include only trials in which an alarm sounded. The result replicated across campaigns: revision C met the limit in 697, 701, and 696 of 720 trials (96.8, 97.4, and 96.7 percent). Treating trials as independent, the 95 percent interval was 96.2 to 97.7 percent, though because trials on the same unit were not fully independent, the true interval is probably somewhat wider. The team also reviewed ward incident reports and found two occlusions, logged by one ward after revision C's release, in which the alarm sounded more than 30 seconds after a nurse noticed flow had stopped. The team could not reproduce delays of that size on the rig, and the reports lacked tubing set and flow rate, so the team treated these reports as unresolved.

The study has clear limits. All trials used room-temperature normal saline; blood, lipid emulsions, other viscous fluids, and air in the line were not tested. The closure rates were chosen to approximate typical blockage dynamics based on published test notes and discussion with network anesthesia staff, and this choice was recorded beforehand, but real patient blockage pressure curves were not measured, so whether the rates bracket clinical conditions remains untested. Only one rig was built, so between-rig variation was not estimated. The team recommends that the network not rely on these results for high-viscosity infusions until a separate viscous-fluid campaign is completed, that revision C firmware be run on at least two independent rigs before any clinical rollout, and that ward incident reports be re-reviewed with flow rate and tubing set recorded. The internal review went to the pump committee in late summer, which requested the raw transducer logs (provided as a sealed archive) and a two-page plain-language summary for ward managers that is not reproduced in the report. The rig was moved to storage after the final campaign and has since been recalibrated, which the report says does not affect the results.

The report documents an acceptance test of a two-layer polyurethane leading-edge coating with ceramic filler (Coating Grade B) for twelve blade sets supplied by Halvane Surface Works to the Ferrow Ridge wind park. Operator Lanterne Energy Group commissioned the test, which the Ostmere Materials Laboratory ran from March to May 2026. The agreed pass line required no more mass loss than the incumbent single-layer Coating Grade A. Older sites using Grade A showed tip pitting after about three seasons, so a rotating-arm rain-erosion rig compared the coatings at 90 metres per second, equal to 400 hours of exposure, with twelve coupons each. Mean mass loss was 41 milligrams for the incumbent and 19 milligrams for the new coating. Both passed, a standard the analysts called lenient. The gap widened after 150 hours, tentatively attributed to filler settling in the outer layer, though this was not measured. Mean roughness rose 0.3 micrometres for the new coating against 1.1 for the incumbent, but its link to power loss is unmeasured. The 95 percent interval on the mass-loss difference runs from about 9 to 35 milligrams, so the true reduction could be much smaller than half. The rig omits hail, UV ageing and thermal cycling, and its droplet size has not been checked for inland sites. Field exposure so far covers only six months. The analysts recommend a two-season field trial on one site, an inland droplet check, and a repeat rig test with a second batch, treating the bench result as a reason to continue rather than proof of improvement.
