This report describes an acceptance test of a two-layer polyurethane leading-edge erosion coating with ceramic filler (Coating Grade B) applied to twelve blade sets for the Ferrow Ridge wind park, operated by Lanterne Energy Group. The test was commissioned by the operator's procurement office, supplied by Halvane Surface Works, and run at the Ostmere Materials Laboratory between March and May 2026. The pass criterion, agreed in advance, was no more mass loss than the incumbent single-layer product (Coating Grade A) under identical conditions. The motivation was pitting near blade tips observed at two older sites after about three seasons of service with the incumbent. The supplier prepared all coupons, and the test used one production batch per product with twelve coupons per arm. Coupons were cut from laminate panels matching the blade shells, cured on the supplier's schedule, and exposed in a rotating-arm rain-erosion rig at a 90 m/s tip speed for 400 equivalent hours, with weighing and profilometry every 50 hours.

At 400 hours, the incumbent coupons lost a mean of 41 mg each and the two-layer coupons lost a mean of 19 mg each. The analysts described this as a possible reduction of roughly half under bench conditions. Both systems met the agreed pass line, which the analysts called lenient. The gap was small for the first 150 hours and widened afterward, which the analysts tentatively attributed to filler settling in the outer layer, though filler distribution was not measured. The report also states that the statistical support is weak: with twelve coupons per arm and large scatter, the 95 percent interval on the difference runs from about 9 to 35 mg, so the true reduction may be much smaller than half. No second batch was tested and only one tip speed was used. Surface roughness rose by 0.3 micrometres for the two-layer coupons against 1.1 micrometres for the incumbent, which the analysts read as a sign of slower surface degradation. They noted that the link between this roughness and power loss has not been measured.

The test covered rain erosion only. Hail, ultraviolet ageing and thermal cycling were not included, so the result should not be read as a general endorsement for the operator's climate range. The rig droplet size matches a coastal study's nozzle specification, but this has not been checked against the inland sites where two new turbines will stand, and lighter inland rain with smaller drops could change the ranking. Field exposure so far is only six months, too short to compare with the incumbent's three-season history, and no pitting measurements exist yet for the new coating. The field team plans inspections at three and six months. The analysts recommend that the procurement office treat the bench result as grounds to continue the trial, not as proof of improvement. Before relying on the results for the wider order, the field trial should run at least two full seasons at one site, the inland droplet assumption should be checked with a short rig run, and a repeat rig test with a second batch and a range of droplet sizes is proposed as the next step.

The Lantern Ridge fraud analytics group evaluated a gradient-boosted classifier for flagging card-not-present transactions, trained on eighteen months of anonymized processor records. On a six-week holdout of about 212,000 transactions with roughly 1,430 confirmed fraud labels, the model reached precision 0.41 at its development threshold, versus 0.27 for the production rules engine. The bootstrap interval spans about 0.35 to 0.47, so the advantage may be considerably smaller. At equal recall it cut manually cleared alerts by about 18 percent, a secondary finding. An offline replay by the operations group, with a slightly different threshold and duplicate handling, produced precision 0.33, so the true gap remains uncertain until duplicate handling is reconciled.

Several limitations apply. Chargebacks can take up to ninety days, so recent true fraud may be labelled legitimate, and unreported fraud is treated as legitimate. Alerts prompting cardholder contact may bias labels toward the model. Velocity features may not reflect a summer timestamp fix, the 40-configuration hyperparameter search was not nested within cross-validation, and the threshold reflects reviewer capacity. Card-present transactions were excluded due to missing device fingerprint fields.

The group does not recommend acting on these results. Before any production change, it requires a replay on a fresh window of at least twelve weeks with labels aged at least ninety days, reconciliation of the duplicate-handling difference, and sign-off from the fraud operations lead that the review queue can absorb the new alert mix.

The Lantern Ridge fraud analytics group evaluated an early gradient-boosted classifier for flagging card-not-present transactions, using eighteen months of anonymized records from a regional card processor under a data-sharing agreement renewed in spring. The work was done by four analysts and one platform engineer. Training code was in Python, run through a platform-group workflow scheduler, with feature tables in a columnar warehouse. Notebooks were peer-reviewed before sharing, a practice adopted after an earlier study was found to have a join error that inflated recall. The internal change log records retraining runs and configurations, and the retrospective archive holds the earlier study's details.

The holdout was six weeks of recent data, containing about 212,000 transactions, of which roughly 1,430 were confirmed fraud after chargeback review. Because chargebacks can take up to ninety days to resolve, recent fraud may be unlabelled and counted as legitimate, and the small positive count makes the results cautious. The first finding is that at the development-selected threshold, the classifier reached precision 0.41 versus 0.27 for the production rules engine, with the gain apparently holding across three merchant categories on small samples. The bootstrap 95% interval for precision spans about 0.35 to 0.47. The second finding is that alerts cleared by manual review fell about 18 percent at equal recall. This rests on the same window and is secondary. The threshold was chosen to match the review team's capacity, accepting lower recall than possible, a business choice the group expects to revisit after a month of use.

The group first tried a logistic baseline, which was abandoned because its feature pipeline broke when the processor changed merchant code formats. Some features, such as rolling velocity counts, depend on timestamp logic revised in summer, and the team has not confirmed that historical features were recomputed with that logic. The evaluation assumes labels are complete and unbiased, which may not hold: unreported fraud would understate the model, while alerts that led reviewers to confirm transactions with cardholders could bias labels in its favour in unmeasured ways. The hyperparameter search covered 40 configurations and was not nested inside cross-validation, so the threshold may be slightly optimistic. Card-present transactions, a little under a third of volume, were excluded because device fingerprint fields are mostly missing, so the results say nothing about that segment.

A separate offline replay by the operations group, at a slightly different threshold, gave precision 0.33, closer to the rules engine. The two runs differ in duplicate-transaction handling, which is not yet reconciled with production, so the true gap could fall anywhere between 0.33 and 0.41. The group recommends three conditions before any production change: a replay on a fresh window of at least twelve weeks with labels aged at least ninety days, reconciliation of the duplicate-handling difference, and sign-off from the fraud operations lead that the review queue can absorb the altered alert mix. The report treats the results as a promising first signal that justifies a longer study, not as a settled judgement, and it advises against acting on them alone. The next report in the series will cover the replay results and whether these conditions were met.

On a six-week holdout of about 212,000 transactions, containing roughly 1,430 confirmed fraud cases after chargeback review, the classifier at the development-selected threshold reached precision 0.41, compared with 0.27 for the production rules engine. The bootstrap 95% interval for precision spans about 0.35 to 0.47. The gain apparently held across three merchant categories, though those samples were small. A secondary finding is that alerts cleared by manual review fell about 18 percent at equal recall over the same window. The threshold was chosen to match review team capacity, which meant accepting lower recall than was possible, and the group expects to revisit it after a month of use.

The text lists several limitations. Chargebacks can take up to ninety days to resolve, so recent fraud may be unlabelled and counted as legitimate, and the small positive count makes the results cautious. The group first tried a logistic baseline but abandoned it when its feature pipeline broke after the processor changed merchant code formats. Some features, such as rolling velocity counts, depend on timestamp logic revised in summer, and the team has not confirmed that historical features were recomputed with that logic. The evaluation assumes labels are complete and unbiased, which may not hold. Unreported fraud would understate performance, and alerts prompting reviewers to confirm transactions with cardholders could bias labels in the model's favour in unmeasured ways. The hyperparameter search covered 40 configurations and was not nested inside cross-validation, so the threshold may be slightly optimistic. Card-present transactions, a little under a third of volume, were excluded because device fingerprint fields are mostly missing, so the results say nothing about that segment.

A separate offline replay by the operations group, at a slightly different threshold, gave precision 0.33, closer to the rules engine. The two runs differ in duplicate-transaction handling, which has not been reconciled with production, so the true gap could lie anywhere between 0.33 and 0.41. The group recommends three conditions before any production change: a replay on a fresh window of at least twelve weeks with labels aged at least ninety days, reconciliation of the duplicate-handling difference, and sign-off from the fraud operations lead that the review queue can absorb the altered alert mix. The report treats the results as a promising first signal that justifies a longer study, not a settled judgement, and advises against acting on them alone. The next report in the series will cover the replay results and whether these conditions were met.
